attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated firmly in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Won't be forthcoming' is a firm forecast with no deadline. The 'not needed' part is evaluative and has no test. The bank and data-center scope matches the sentence before it.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: an executed, exceptional US rescue of lenders or their distressed AI data-center exposure. It correctly says that no bailout so far cannot confirm an undated negative forecast.

evidence.note: DOE money for grid upgrades. This is ordinary infrastructure support, not a rescue of distressed lenders, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The packet shows no qualifying US bailout by the evaluation date, and the only official funding item is ordinary grid support. With no deadline, no bailout so far does not confirm the forecast, and no conclusive event contradicts it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. The 89% figure appears to come from The Information's survey, but he states it in his own voice.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps both linked figures, the 'at best' ceiling, and the exclusion rule.

contract.note: The 89% plainly echoes an annualised tally of 34 startups. Requiring realized revenue for the year to March 2026, with whole-industry coverage, is a reading the speaker did not give and leans against him. The result depends on the basis and the universe chosen.

evidence.note: Reports 89% of annualised revenue across 34 startups, excluding listed firms and AI cloud firms. That basis and universe differ from the contract's realized whole-industry test, and it does not establish the $20B ceiling.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence matches the 89% on an annualised startup-sample basis, not on the contract's realized basis. Nothing establishes total revenue for the rest of the industry against the $20B ceiling. The contract's evaluator-chosen basis is also arguably unfair, so the case cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, stated firmly in his own voice.

semantics.note: It keeps the mechanism, the doubling and the under-10-months window. It drops the side claim that all electronics got more expensive, but the core causal claim is intact.

contract.note: Asking for comparable cost estimates and memory-driven causation is a fair, ordinary reading of 'doubled the cost'.

evidence.note: Independent evidence of tight memory supply driven by AI. It does not measure data-center cost per GW.
A March forecast of NAND and DRAM price rises, not realized project costs.
A secondary summary of Huang's roughly $100B-per-GW estimate. There is no matched $50B baseline and no cost breakdown.

reviews.rationale: The packet backs the memory-price pressure and the $100B end figure. But there is no comparable $50B baseline inside the window, no matched specifications, and no breakdown attributing the rise to RAM and storage. Neither the doubling nor its cause is established.

attribution.note: Zitron's own estimate and inference, in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I estimate at least 70%' gives a firm numeric threshold, not graded confidence, so it is checkable. The inference about money flows is mixed causal and observation, and the hedges are preserved.

contract.note: Reading 'entire AI industry' broadly is ordinary, and the contract flags the Q1 period and intercompany counting as open. The result depends on how the denominator is bounded.

evidence.note: A 15–20% share of compute capacity at end-2025 is a different metric and period from a revenue share.
OpenAI's own announcement of funding commitments. It gives no revenue ratio or Q1 spending.
OpenAI's Q1 cash burn is not compute spend. Nothing on Anthropic or the industry total.

reviews.rationale: Neither the combined Q1 compute spend nor a defined industry revenue denominator is established, and nothing traces where the funding went. Every item is a different metric or a partial measure, so the 70% ratio and the funding-flow claim are both unresolved.
